title: Light-Head R-CNN: In Defense of Two-Stage Object Detector

problem.summary: Typical two-stage detectors are slower than fast single-stage detectors because their heads are heavy: Faster R-CNN runs two large fully connected layers per RoI and R-FCN must generate huge score maps around RoI warping, so shrinking the backbone does not proportionally reduce computation and no fast two-stage detector with competitive accuracy exists.
statements: Faster R-CNN and R-FCN perform intensive computation before or after RoI warping due to their heavy-head design.
Per-region prediction is time-consuming and worsens as the number of proposals grows.
The large channel count after ROI pooling makes the first fully connected layer memory-hungry and slows the network.
Reducing the base model alone does not largely decrease computation cost.
Object detection lacks a competitive fast two-stage detector with near single-stage speed.

evidence.quote: We find that Faster RCNN [28] and R-FCN [17] perform an intensive computation after or before RoI warping.

Faster R-CNN involves two fully connected layers for RoI recognition, while RFCN produces a large score maps. Thus, the speed of these networks is slow due to the heavy-head design in the architecture.
Even if we significantly reduce the base model, the computation cost cannot be largely decreased accordingly.
It is time-consuming in terms of per-region prediction and even gets worse when a large number of proposals are utilized.
In addition, the number of feature channels after ROI pooling is large, which makes the first fully connected consume a large memory and potentially influence the computational speed.
object detection literature is lack of competitive fast two-stage detector compared single-stage approaches with nearly accuracy.

background.summary: The work builds on the R-CNN lineage (Selective Search proposals, Fast R-CNN multi-task training, Faster R-CNN's RPN, R-FCN's shared computation) plus FPN/Mask R-CNN/RetinaNet and the fast single-stage line (YOLO, SSD, DSSD, DeNet); the claimed gap is that accuracy-oriented two-stage designs kept making heads heavier while speed-oriented work focused on single-stage detectors.

relatedWork.name: R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: first to put deep neural network features into a detection system
relatedWork.quote: R-CNN [6] is among the first to utilize deep neural network features into detection system.

relatedWork.name: Fast R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: joins classification and box regression into one multi-task trained model
relatedWork.quote: Then Fast R-CNN [5] is proposed to join train object classification and bounding box regression, which improves the performance by multi-task training.

relatedWork.name: Faster R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: milestone two-stage detector whose RPN generates proposals from network features
relatedWork.quote: Following Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN [28] introduces Region Proposal Network (RPN) to generate proposals by using network features.

relatedWork.name: R-FCN
relatedWork.relation: shares computation across RoIs to speed up inference with many proposals
relatedWork.quote: R-FCN [17] shares computations between RoI subnetworks, which speed up inference when a large number of proposals are utilized.

relatedWork.name: FPN
relatedWork.relation: multiscale pyramidal feature construction that later designs build on
relatedWork.quote: Lin et al. propose Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) [19], which exploits inherent multiscale, pyramidal hierarchy of deep convolutional networks to construct feature pyramids.

relatedWork.name: RetinaNet
relatedWork.relation: FPN-based single-stage detector addressing foreground-background imbalance with Focal Loss
relatedWork.quote: RetinaNet [20] is another FPN based single stage detector, which involves Focal-Loss to address class imbalance issue caused by extreme foreground-background ratio.

relatedWork.name: YOLO / SSD
relatedWork.relation: proposal-free single-stage detectors that treat detection as regression over boxes
relatedWork.quote: YOLO and YOLO v2 [26, 27] simplifies object detection as a regression problem, which directly predicts the bounding boxes and associated class probabilities without proposal generation.

evidence.quote: We briefly review some of the recent object detection work in two dimensions as follows:
Hand-engineered methods, such as Selective Search [37], Edge Boxes [40], MCG[1], is involved to generate proposals for R-CNN.

solution.summary: Light-Head R-CNN makes the head as light as possible: a large-kernel separable convolution produces thin feature maps (10 x p x p channels) before RoI warping, and a cheap R-CNN subnet with a single fully connected layer does per-RoI recognition, instantiated in a large-backbone Setting L (ResNet-101) and a small-backbone Setting S (Xception-like).
solution.approach: Shrink the channels available to the RoI-wise subnetwork with thin feature maps from large separable convolutions and replace the heavy per-region subnetwork with a single cheap fully connected layer.
components: thin feature maps (alpha x p x p channels, alpha <= 10) produced by large separable convolution (k = 15)
cheap R-CNN subnet: one fully connected layer with 2048 channels (no dropout) after pooling
Setting L with ResNet-101 backbone and Setting S with a tiny Xception-like backbone
PSRoI pooling with interpolation (RoIAlign-style) for Setting L; PSPooling with alignment for Setting S
anchor scheme of 3 aspect ratios and 5 scales with 0.7 IoU NMS and OHEM training
multi-scale training, relaxed 0.5 NMS threshold, and àtrous stage-5 convolutions

evidence.quote: We propose a new two-stage detector, Light-Head RCNN, to address the shortcoming in current two-stage approaches.
In our design, we make the head of network as light as possible, by using a thin feature map and a cheap R-CNN subnet (pooling and single fully-connected layer).
we apply a large-kernel separable convolution to produce “thin” feature maps with small channel number (α × p × p is used in our experiments and α ≤ 10).
In our experiments, we find that RoI warping on thin feature maps will not only improves the accuracy but also saves memory and computation during training and inference.
A cheap single fully-connected layer is attached to the pooling layer, which well exploits the feature representation for classification and regression.

experiments.summary: Evaluated on COCO (115k train + 5k mini-validation for ablations, test-dev for final numbers) with ResNet-101 ablations over baselines, thin maps, large kernel, and light R-CNN subnet, then compared against FPN, Mask R-CNN, RetinaNet and fast detectors; the fast variant swaps in a tiny Xception-like backbone and reports FPS alongside mAP.

benchmarks.split: mini-validation, full recipe incl. multiscale train
test-dev, Light head R-CNN ms-train, single-scale test
test-dev, best Light head R-CNN row

evidence.quote: In this section, we evaluate our approach on COCO [21, 18] dataset, which has 80 object categories.
Our detector is end-to-end trained based on 8 Pascal TITAN XP GPUs using synchronized SGD with a weight decay of 0.0001 and momentum of 0.9.
Our single scale tested model can achieve 40.8% mmAP without bells and whistles, significantly surpassing all the competitors (40.8 vs 39.1).
Multi-scale training brings nearly 1 points improvement on mmAP.
our methods get 30.7 mmAP at 102 FPS on MS COCO, significantly outperforming the fast detectors like YOLO and SSD.

limitations.summary: Thinning the feature maps alone slightly hurts accuracy until the large kernel and light subnet are added; the fast model relies on a deliberately small backbone and a non-pre-activation design, and the authors note RoI-align would do better than their PSPooling-with-alignment choice.
items: Thin feature maps by themselves reduce mmAP (32.1 to 31.4 and 35.2 to 34.6); gains need the large kernel and light R-CNN subnet.
The fast Setting S abandons àtrous convolution and uses a non-pre-activation Xception-like backbone because it is shallow.
The speed headline (30.7 mAP at 102 FPS) comes from a much weaker backbone than the 41.5 mAP ResNet-101 model.
PSPooling with alignment is used instead of RoI-align, which the authors expect to perform better.

evidence.quote: Although the channel number has been largely decrease, 3969 vs 490, our have comparable performance.
However we do not use the pre-activation design which is proposed in identity mappings [10] because of shallow network.
Larger backbone like Resnet 101 is slow based on the computational speed.
Noticing that it will obtain better results if we involve RoI-align.

futureDirections.direction: Use RoI-align instead of the current pooling scheme for further accuracy gains in the fast setting.
futureDirections.quote: Noticing that it will obtain better results if we involve RoI-align.

equations.name: thin feature map channels
equations.expr: Cout = alpha x p x p with alpha <= 10 (10 x p x p used in experiments)

applications.detail: Authors from Megvii position Light-Head R-CNN as a two-stage detector that keeps time efficiency, with a tiny-backbone variant reported at 102 FPS and 30.7 mAP on COCO.
applications.quote: Our ResNet-101 based light-head R-CNN outperforms state-of-art object detectors on COCO while keeping time efficiency.

deploymentClaims: 30.7 mmAP at 102 FPS on COCO test-dev with a small Xception-like backbone (700/1100 test size).
31.5 mmAP at 95 FPS with the same fast backbone at 800/1200 test size.
Single-scale 40.8 mmAP on test-dev with ResNet-101, surpassing RetinaNet ms-train (39.1).

evidence.quote: Code will be made publicly available.
our Light Head R-CNN coupled with small Xception-like base model can achieve 30.7 mmAP at the speed of 102 FPS.
